Breath
breth
n. (rendering Hebrew neshamah/ruach, Greek pnoē)
From Saxon braeth, breath, vapour, exhalation. Hebrew has two words the English merges: neshamah, the breath of life God breathed into man's nostrils, and ruach, wind, breath, or spirit. Greek pnoē is a blowing or breath, from pneō, to blow, the root of pneuma.

Biblical Definition

Breath in Scripture is the borrowed thing on which every living creature depends moment by moment. Elihu states both the origin and the ownership: “The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life” (Job 33:4). Paul preaches the same doctrine to philosophers on Mars' hill, and draws from it the uselessness of temples built to supply God's needs: “he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things” (Acts 17:25). Because breath is a gift and not a possession, the mere fact of having it constitutes an obligation, and the Psalter ends on exactly that note: “Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD” (Psalm 150:6) — the last verse of the book, and the widest command in it. And breath is what God supplies when He raises the dead: in the valley of dry bones the sinews and flesh come first and the corpses still do not live until He says, “Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live” (Ezekiel 37:5). That order is the doctrine of regeneration in a vision. A man may be assembled, instructed, and outwardly complete, and remain a corpse until God breathes; and when He does, the life is undeniably His and not the bones'.

Webster 1828 Definition

The air drawn into and expelled from the lungs; the life that depends on it. In Scripture, the breath of the Almighty that gives life, God giving to all life and breath, everything that hath breath commanded to praise the LORD, and the breath He causes to enter dry bones that they may live.

expand to see more

BREATH, n. 1. The air inhaled and expelled in the respiration of animals.

2. Life; the power of respiring, and hence, existence itself.

3. A single respiration; hence a moment, an instant; also a gentle breeze.

4. From Saxon braeth, an exhalation, vapour, breath.

5. In Scripture, the breath of the Almighty hath given me life, Job 33; let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD, Ps. 150.

Key Scripture

Job 33:4 — "The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life."

Acts 17:25 — "Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things;"

Psalm 150:6 — "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD."

Ezekiel 37:5 — "Thus saith the Lord GOD unto these bones; Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live:"

Modern Corruption

Life is treated as a property the creature owns, so that its beginning and end become matters of human choice; and the divine breath is reduced to a metaphor for an impersonal life-force shared by all things.

expand to see more

If breath is given moment by moment by God, then life is held on loan and no man is proprietor of his own or another's. That single premise stands against the age at both ends of life. The unborn child, whose members were written in God's book before they were formed, is not disposable tissue; the aged and the suffering, whose breath God still gives, are not candidates for a managed exit dressed up as dignity. Daniel put it to Belshazzar without softening: “the God in whose hand thy breath is, and whose are all thy ways, hast thou not glorified” (Daniel 5:23). Every argument for autonomy over life begins by denying that clause, and the denial is not usually stated — it is assumed, and then the ethics follow easily.

The second corruption runs the other way, dissolving the personal Giver into an impersonal energy. Panentheist and process theologies make the divine breath the animating principle immanent in all things, so that God is the life of the world rather than its Creator, and the difference between Him and His creatures is one of degree. Scripture keeps the distinction absolute: God gives breath, and He is not Himself the breath He gives; He is aseity itself, needing nothing, worshipped not with men's hands as though He needed any thing. The practical difference is the whole of religion. An impersonal life-force cannot be praised, cannot be sinned against, and cannot raise the dead — and the LORD who breathed into Adam's nostrils, and who breathes upon dry bones, does all three.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew neshamah, the breath of life breathed into man; ruach, breath, wind, or spirit; Greek pnoē, a breath or blowing, and pneuma, spirit.

expand to see more

Hebrew neshamah (H5397) — breath, especially the breath of life God breathed into Adam (Genesis 2:7); also the spirit of man as the candle of the LORD (Proverbs 20:27).

Hebrew ruach (H7307) — wind, breath, spirit; the word of Ezekiel 37, where wind, breath, and Spirit are the same term.

Greek pnoē (G4157) — breath, a blowing; used of God giving breath (Acts 17:25) and of the rushing mighty wind at Pentecost (Acts 2:2).

Greek pneuma (G4151) — spirit, breath, wind; the Holy Ghost, and the human spirit rendered up at death.

Greek theopneustos (G2315) — God-breathed; the adjective describing Scripture in 2 Timothy 3:16.

Usage

"Of life as a gift constantly given: he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things (Acts 17:25)."

"Of the universal obligation to praise: Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD (Psalm 150:6)."

"Of resurrection and regeneration: I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live (Ezekiel 37:5)."
